Who values, taxes and bills Wyoming homes?

Three layers handle a Wyoming tax bill. Your county assessor puts a value on the house. Local governments pick the mill levies. Your county treasurer sends the bill and takes the payment. The Property Tax Division at the state Department of Revenue trains the local offices and values utility property such as pipelines, railroads and telecommunications. Homeowners do not pay that division anything, so every residential payment goes to the treasurer.

Lawmakers fix the assessment ratio. Homes are assessed at 9.5 percent of market value, industrial property at 11.5 percent and minerals at 100 percent of fair market value. School districts, hospital districts, towns and counties each levy the mills their budgets call for.

When you plan to sell, remember that value, rate and bill come from separate offices. Value questions belong with the assessor, payment questions with the treasurer.

How a Wyoming tax bill is figured

Take market value, apply the assessment ratio, then apply the mill levy and divide by 1,000. One mill is $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessed value.

For 2025 the average levy across the state was 65.280 mills. Teton County had the lowest county average at 57.772 and Big Horn County the highest at 73.826. Natrona County came in at 72.238 and Weston County at 73.210. Because the district mix differs from place to place, two homes worth the same can carry quite different yearly bills, and buyers weigh that figure when they shop.

Roughly 30 percent of assessed value statewide is residential and roughly 44 percent is minerals. Look on your treasurer's bill to see the levy on your parcel.

The 25 percent homeowner exemption

Senate Enrolled Act 60, passed in 2025, trims a home's taxable value by 25 percent on fair market value up to $1 million. There is no sunset date. The bill came without replacement money for schools, special districts or local governments that lose revenue.

Houses, condominiums, townhouses and manufactured homes qualify when the owner lives in them eight or more months of the year. Some military members who fall short of that may still be eligible. Filing means an affidavit delivered to the county assessor. In the second year the Department of Revenue pushed the deadline to March 1 from February 1, so phone the assessor for the date that applies now. Owners on the long-term homeowners exemption cannot take the 25 percent reduction until tax year 2027.

Refunds, veteran and senior relief

Wyoming offers three other programs alongside the 25 percent exemption. They run through separate applications and separate offices, so learn which of them the seller already has.

  • Property tax refund: aimed at homeowners who have trouble paying. A household at or below 125 percent of county median income gets back 75 percent of the taxes it paid, with a cap of half the county's median residential bill. Eligibility ends at 145 percent of county median income, and households between 126 and 145 percent get that amount cut by 35 percent.
  • Veteran exemption: went up from $3,000 to $6,000 in 2024.
  • Senior relief: a 50 percent reduction for Wyomingites 65 or older with at least 25 years of Wyoming property tax payments.

Refund applications go through wptrs.wyo.gov. The 2025 Legislature put $10.5 million more into the refund fund; call the state office to learn the current round and its dates.

Valuation date and appealing your assessment

Property in Wyoming is listed, valued and assessed on January 1. A challenge starts at the county assessor's office. In Laramie County, assessment schedules go out by the fourth Monday in April, and a written objection has to be in the assessor's hands within 30 days of that mailing.

Next the county board of equalization rules on current-year protests, in writing, by October 1. W.S. 39-13-109(b)(i) lets the board either uphold the assessor or side with the taxpayer. After that the road leads to the State Board of Equalization and finally district court.

The appeal is about market value, not the rate, and it needs backing for your figure. Sellers can submit a fresh appraisal, pictures of damage the assessor missed, or a signed contract showing what a buyer agreed to pay.

Due dates and penalties

The bill comes in two installments, and anything late collects 18 percent interest per year. Laramie County mails its notices on the last business day of August.

InstallmentDuePay by
First halfSeptember 1November 10
Second halfMarch 1May 10 of the next year

Settle everything by December 31 and the first-half interest is waived. Once May 11 passes without payment, the treasurer certifies a delinquent list and sends a demand notice about five business days after. Not receiving the bill is no defense.

Many homeowners rely on mortgage escrow. If a lender and an owner both pay in Laramie County, the treasurer holds the first and refunds the second. Ask the treasurer before listing whether your escrow money really posted.

What happens if Wyoming property tax goes unpaid?

Real property tax that goes unpaid turns into a standing lien, and the county may auction the property. W.S. 39-13-108 puts that lien ahead of every claimant except the United States and the State of Wyoming.

  • The treasurer publishes notice weekly for three weeks in a legal newspaper, starting no less than four weeks before the auction date.
  • The auction is held at the county courthouse, any day but Sunday, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • The winning bidder covers the tax, interest, penalties and costs and receives a certificate of purchase.
  • If nobody bids the amount owed, the county treasurer bids on the county's behalf.
  • If the owner never redeems, a tax deed may follow four years after the sale. Occupants, owners and mortgagees must first receive notice three months or more in advance.

The treasurer can confirm current steps. Dealing with a delinquency early keeps more choices open.

Taxes at the time of sale

Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure, then have the closing agent pay it from your proceeds. Because the tax is a lien on the land and building, it travels with the house until someone pays it.

W.S. 34-1-142 calls for the deed to be recorded with the county clerk together with a sworn statement from the grantee or the grantee's agent. The statement gives price and terms, stays confidential, and may be shown only to a person reviewing or contesting a property tax assessment.

Exemptions may not follow the house to the buyer. The 25 percent break turns on the owner living there, so a new owner may need to file a fresh affidavit.

If you inherited the house, note that the small estate limit rose to $400,000 on July 1, 2025. That can shorten the transfer when real property sits inside a modest estate.

Pre-listing checklist: payoff figure from the treasurer, proof that both installments are handled, confirmation that any escrow money posted, and a word with the assessor about exemptions on file. An open tax bill does not stop a cash sale, since the balance is settled out of proceeds like any other lien.

Frequently asked questions

What percent of market value is Wyoming residential property assessed at?

Assessors count 9.5 percent of a home's market value. The ratios for industry and minerals are higher, 11.5 percent and 100 percent.

What is the Wyoming average mill levy?

For tax year 2025 the statewide average was 65.280 mills. County averages ran from 57.772 in Teton County to 73.826 in Big Horn County.

How do I qualify for the 25 percent homeowner exemption?

You need to own the house, occupy it eight months or more each year, and send an affidavit to the county assessor. Value above $1 million gets no reduction.

What interest does Wyoming charge on late property tax?

Interest runs at 18 percent a year on late balances. A full payment made before the year ends, by December 31, erases first-half interest.

Where do I appeal a Wyoming property assessment?

Go to the county assessor first, inside 30 days of the assessment schedule mailing. After that the county board of equalization decides by October 1.
